claim: Two tumors (284 and 159) from a dataset of 140 nominal ccRCC samples were identified as metabolic outliers by t-SNE analysis.
source: Specifically, multidimensional similarity analysis using t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) indicated that tumors 284 and 159 clustered separately from the 138 other tumors in the RC12 dataset (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from t-SNE analysis shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: Tumors 284 and 159 were pathologically confirmed to be CCPAP tumors upon re-review.
source: Pathologic re-review of these metabolic outliers identified them as bearing morphology and immunohistochemical profile characteristic of CCPAP tumors.
evidence: The claim is based on pathological re-review of the tumor samples.

claim: CCPAP tumors exhibit approximately thirty-fold accumulation of sorbitol relative to adjacent normal kidney.
source: Interestingly, the primary metabolic feature which distinguished these tumors from the ccRCC samples was the approximately thirty-fold accumulation (relative to levels in adjacent normal kidney) of the sugar alcohol sorbitol.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements comparing CCPAP tumors to normal kidney tissue.

claim: CCPAP samples form a distinct cluster from ccRCC tumors and adjacent-normal tissue in t-SNE analysis of metabolomic data.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, using t-SNE analysis, CCPAP samples again formed a distinct cluster from conventional ccRCC tumors and from adjacent-normal tissue.
evidence: The claim is supported by t-SNE analysis of metabolomic data from the RC13 validation cohort shown in Figure 1B.

claim: High-sorbitol ccRCC tumors cluster with other ccRCC tumors and not with CCPAP samples in t-SNE analysis.
source: Importantly, to evaluate the possibility that sorbitol levels were excessively contributing to the t-SNE analysis, we also included two ccRCC samples from RC12 with aberrantly high sorbitol levels comparable to those from the other RC12 CCPAP samples. We observed that high-sorbitol ccRCC tumors clustered with other ccRCC tumors and not with CCPAP samples.
evidence: The claim is based on t-SNE analysis that included high-sorbitol ccRCC samples as controls.

claim: 200 metabolites were identified as differentially abundant between CCPAP and ccRCC samples with q value < 0.1 and greater than 2-fold change.
source: After adjusting for multiple-hypothesis testing, we identified 200 differentially abundant metabolites with q value < 0.1 and a greater than 2-fold change relative to ccRCC (non-parametric Mann-Whitney test, Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of metabolomic data using Mann-Whitney test with multiple hypothesis correction.

claim: 152 metabolites were differentially abundant in CCPAP compared to adjacent normal kidney tissue.
source: Of these, 152 were differentially abundant compared to adjacent normal kidney tissue, confirming the CCPAP-specific nature of these metabolic changes (at least 2-fold change and q < 0.1, Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical comparison of metabolite abundances between CCPAP and normal tissue.

claim: Sorbitol exhibits an approximately 8.5-fold increase in CCPAP samples compared to ccRCC samples.
source: Among these, sorbitol was among the metabolites with the largest change in abundance, exhibiting an approximately 8.5-fold increase in CCPAP samples compared to ccRCC samples (64-fold when excluding the atypical, high-sorbitol ccRCC samples) and a 36-fold elevation compared to normal tissue (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative metabolomic measurements shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: Sorbitol exhibits a 36-fold elevation in CCPAP compared to normal tissue.
source: Among these, sorbitol was among the metabolites with the largest change in abundance, exhibiting an approximately 8.5-fold increase in CCPAP samples compared to ccRCC samples (64-fold when excluding the atypical, high-sorbitol ccRCC samples) and a 36-fold elevation compared to normal tissue (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative metabolomic measurements shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: Three other sugar alcohols (palatinitol, erythritol, and ribitol) were elevated approximately 4-fold or greater in CCPAP compared to ccRCC.
source: Three other sugar alcohols (palatinitol, erythritol, and ribitol) were also elevated approximately 4-fold or greater in CCPAP compared to ccRCC (>5 fold when excluding atypical, high-sorbitol ccRCC samples, Figure 2—source data 1), suggesting that a metabolic pathway associated with production or degradation of polyols is differentially active in CCPAP tumors.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements of sugar alcohols.

claim: CCPAP tumors have significantly elevated levels (>12 fold) of both reduced and oxidized glutathione (GSH and GSSG).
source: Notably, CCPAP tumors had significantly elevated levels (>12 fold) of both reduced and oxidized glutathione (GSH and GSSG), the cell's primary anti-oxidants.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements of glutathione levels.

claim: CCPAP tumors show a 4-fold increase in ophthalmate relative to ccRCC.
source: Increases in abundance of other metabolites involved in the response to oxidative stress were also evident, for example a 4-fold increase in ophthalmate relative to ccRCC (with even greater elevation relative to normal tissue) (Figure 2A and D, Figure 2—source data 1) (Soga et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements and cited literature on ophthalmate's role in oxidative stress.

claim: A variety of lipids, especially glycerophosphoethanolamines, were broadly downregulated in CCPAP relative to both ccRCC and normal tissue.
source: In contrast, a variety of lipids, especially in the class of glycerophosphoethanolamines, were broadly downregulated in CCPAP relative to both ccRCC and normal tissue (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements of lipid classes shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ccRCC tumors exhibit elevated levels of glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) and fructose-6-phosphate (F6P) compared to normal tissue.
source: While ccRCC tumors exhibit elevated levels of several metabolites in upper glycolysis (e.g. glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) and fructose-6-phosphate (F6P)), levels of G6P and F6P in CCPAP were not different from normal.
evidence: The claim is based on metabolomic measurements comparing ccRCC to normal tissue.

claim: Levels of G6P and F6P in CCPAP were not different from normal tissue.
source: While ccRCC tumors exhibit elevated levels of several metabolites in upper glycolysis (e.g. glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) and fructose-6-phosphate (F6P)), levels of G6P and F6P in CCPAP were not different from normal.
evidence: The claim is based on metabolomic measurements comparing CCPAP to normal tissue.

claim: Levels of sorbitol and fructose were elevated >30 fold in CCPAP relative to normal tissue.
source: In contrast, levels of sorbitol and fructose, the metabolites of polyol pathway, were elevated >30 fold in CCPAP relative to normal tissue.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements of polyol pathway metabolites.

claim: Fructose levels were 5-fold higher in CCPAP than in ccRCC.
source: While fructose levels were also elevated in ccRCC (compared to normal), the levels of fructose were 5-fold higher in CCPAP than in ccRCC (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements comparing CCPAP and ccRCC.

claim: The NADH/NAD ratio was elevated in CCPAP tumors compared to normal tissue.
source: We also observed that the NADH/NAD ratio, a measure of redox potential of the cell and a potential readout of respiratory chain function, was also elevated in CCPAP tumors compared to normal tissue (Figure 2B and D, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements of NADH and NAD levels.

claim: Five suspected cases of CCPAP (BP-4760, BP-4784, BP-4795, DV-5567, BP-4177) were identified during re-review by TCGA panel pathologists.
source: Five suspected cases of CCPAP (BP-4760, BP-4784, BP-4795, DV-5567, BP-4177) were identified during re-review by the TCGA panel pathologists, including two at our institution as part of the TCGA effort and excluded from the final TCGA manuscript (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on pathological re-review of TCGA samples.

claim: The most significantly down-regulated gene-sets in CCPAP compared to normal tissue or ccRCC were associated with oxygen-dependent mitochondrial metabolism.
source: Among these, we observed that the most significantly down-regulated gene-sets enriched in either the gN or gC lists were associated with oxygen-dependent mitochondrial metabolism (e.g., 'MOOTHA_MITOCHONDRIA' 'HALLMARK_ OXIDATIVE_PHOSPHORYLATION') (Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of transcriptomic data.

claim: Several of the most significantly up-regulated gene-sets in CCPAP compared to normal tissue were associated with the hypoxic response.
source: Furthermore, several of the most significantly up-regulated gene-sets enriched in the gN list of differentially expressed genes were associated with the hypoxic response (e.g., ELVIDGE_HYPOXIA_UP, q value < 10−5) (Figure 3—source data 1), consistent with previous findings that HIF is upregulated in CCPAP (Rohan et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis and is consistent with prior literature on HIF upregulation in CCPAP.

claim: Two CCPAP tumors (BP-4760 and BP-4795) were among the four samples lowest in mtDNA copy number in the TCGA ccRCC dataset.
source: Re-examining this data, we found that the 2 CCPAP tumors were among the four samples lowest in mtDNA copy number (Figure 3A, Mann-Whitney p-value 0.016).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of mtDNA copy number from TCGA sequencing data.

claim: CCPAP samples exhibited a > 2 fold reduction in mtRNA levels compared to ccRCC tumor samples.
source: In agreement with our finding of mtDNA depletion, CCPAP samples exhibited a > 2 fold reduction in mtRNA levels compared to ccRCC tumor samples (t-test using TPM estimates from Reznik et al., 2017, p-value 0.0002, Figure 3B) and a > 3 fold reduction in mtRNA levels compared to adjacent-normal tissue in the KIRC study (p-value 10−6, Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of mtRNA expression levels from RNA-sequencing data.

claim: CCPAP samples exhibited a > 3 fold reduction in mtRNA levels compared to adjacent-normal tissue.
source: In agreement with our finding of mtDNA depletion, CCPAP samples exhibited a > 2 fold reduction in mtRNA levels compared to ccRCC tumor samples (t-test using TPM estimates from Reznik et al., 2017, p-value 0.0002, Figure 3B) and a > 3 fold reduction in mtRNA levels compared to adjacent-normal tissue in the KIRC study (p-value 10−6, Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of mtRNA expression levels from RNA-sequencing data.

claim: Of 852 nuclear-DNA encoded, mitochondrially-localizing genes expressed in CCPAP tumors, 411 were downregulated and 99 were upregulated compared to normal tissues.
source: Analysis using nuclear-DNA encoded, mitochondrially-localizing genes (rather than genes encoded in the mitochondrial genome) yielded similar results: of the 852 genes in the Mitochondrion GO geneset and expressed at a minimal level in CCPAP tumors, 411 were downregulated and 99 were upregulated in CCPAP tumors compared to normal tissues (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes.

claim: The abundance of aspartate was reduced 3.5-fold in CCPAP relative to adjacent normal tissues.
source: Consistent with the down-regulation of mitochondrial function due to mtDNA depletion, we found when re-visiting CCPAP metabolomics data that the abundance of aspartate, a metabolite whose abundance is dependent on normal function of the mitochondrial respiratory chain for its production, was reduced 3.5-fold in CCPAP relative to adjacent normal tissues (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements of aspartate levels.

claim: Fumarate was reduced 4-fold in CCPAP relative to normal tissue.
source: Fumarate, another metabolite typically considered to mitochondria-specific, was also reduced 4-fold in CCPAP relative to normal tissue (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements of fumarate levels.

claim: CCPAP tumors have a characteristically low mutational burden when compared to ccRCC tumors.
source: The results of the sequencing analysis revealed that CCPAP tumors have a characteristically low mutational burden when compared to ccRCC tumors (Figure 4A, Figure 3—source data 2), and that all CCPAP tumors were both VHL and TCEB1 wild type.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing data comparing CCPAP and ccRCC.

claim: All CCPAP tumors were both VHL and TCEB1 wild type.
source: The results of the sequencing analysis revealed that CCPAP tumors have a characteristically low mutational burden when compared to ccRCC tumors (Figure 4A, Figure 3—source data 2), and that all CCPAP tumors were both VHL and TCEB1 wild type.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing analysis of CCPAP tumors.

claim: No single gene was non-synonymously mutated in more than one CCPAP sample.
source: Furthermore, we failed to identify a single gene which was non-synonymously mutated in more than one sample.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of somatic mutations across CCPAP samples.

claim: CCPAP tumors are remarkably 'copy-number quiet,' exhibiting few if any focal copy number alterations and no arm-level copy number alterations.
source: Finally, using an allele-specific copy number detection algorithm (FACETS) (Shen and Seshan, 2016), we found that CCPAP tumors are remarkably 'copy-number quiet,' exhibiting few if any focal copy number alterations and no arm-level copy number alterations (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by copy number analysis using the FACETS algorithm.

claim: CCPAP tumors are approximately ~10 fold depleted of mtDNA relative to normal kidney.
source: Relative to normal kidney, we found that CCPAP tumors are approximately ~10 fold depleted of mtDNA (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by estimation of mtDNA copy number from sequencing data.

claim: No non-synonymous mutations were found in mtDNA maintenance genes in CCPAP tumors.
source: Using a manually curated list of genes (Figure 4—source data 1) known to lead to mtDNA depletion or other mtDNA-associated disorders, we evaluated the possibility that these genes may be somatically inactivated (i.e. by truncating or otherwise loss-of-function mutations) in CCPAP tumors. We found no non-synonymous mutations in any gene in our manually curated list.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of somatic mutations in a curated list of mtDNA maintenance genes.

claim: No mtDNA maintenance genes were significantly (q < 0.05) differentially expressed in CCPAP relative to both ccRCC and adjacent-normal tissue.
source: Using the results of our differential gene expression analysis, we found no mtDNA maintenance genes which were significantly (q < 0.05) differentially expressed in CCPAP relative to both ccRCC and adjacent-normal tissue.
evidence: The claim is based on differential gene expression analysis of mtDNA maintenance genes.

claim: Ultra-deep duplex sequencing of mtDNA in CCPAP tumors revealed <1 non-synonymous somatic mutation per sequenced tumor.
source: As shown in Figure 4E, we observed a handful of non-synonymous mtDNA mutations, with a frequency of <1 non-synonymous somatic mutation per sequenced tumor.
evidence: The claim is supported by ultra-deep duplex sequencing of mtDNA.

claim: All identified mtDNA coding variants in CCPAP were missense mutations and were not annotated to have deleterious consequences.
source: All identified coding variants were missense mutations, and were not annotated in the literature to have deleterious consequences (using MITOMAP [Lott et al., 2013]).
evidence: The claim is based on annotation of mtDNA variants using the MITOMAP database.

claim: CCPAP cases co-localized with adjacent-normal kidney tissue rather than ccRCC tumor samples in principal components analysis of DNA methylation data.
source: Principal components analysis of this data indicated that CCPAP cases did not cluster separately, but instead co-localized with adjacent-normal kidney tissue, rather than ccRCC tumor samples.
evidence: The claim is supported by principal components analysis of TCGA methylation data.

claim: The intensity of both TOM20 and MT-CO1 was significantly lower in CCPAP compared with ccRCC and adjacent normal tissue.
source: Consistent with our prior results, we found that the intensity of both TOM20 and MT-CO1 was significantly lower in CCPAP compared with ccRCC and adjacent normal tissue (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining and quantification.

claim: CCPAP has the lowest MT-CO1 H-score among different subtypes of renal cell carcinoma.
source: A more comprehensive quantification using tissue array samples from different subtypes of renal cell carcinoma also confirmed that CCPAP has the lowest MT-CO1 H-score (Figure 3—source data 2, Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemical analysis across RCC subtypes.

claim: The miR200 family (miR200a,b,c, miR429) are upregulated in CCPAP relative to ccRCC.
source: Moreover, microRNA analysis showed that the miR200 family (miR200a,b,c, miR429), which has been shown to be induced by oxidative stress and which suppresses the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), are upregulated in CCPAP relative to ccRCC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—source data 1), consistent with a previous report (Lawrie et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by microRNA analysis and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: The intensity of 8-oxo-dG was higher in CCPAP compared with ccRCC and adjacent normal tissue.
source: We found that the intensity of 8-oxo-dG was higher in CCPAP compared with ccRCC and adjacent normal tissue (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining for 8-oxo-dG.

claim: CCPAP has the highest 8-oxo-dG H-score among different subtypes of renal cell carcinoma.
source: A more comprehensive quantification using tissue array samples comprised of different subtypes of renal cell carcinoma also showed CCPAP has the highest 8-oxo-dG H-score (Figure 5D, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemical analysis across RCC subtypes.

claim: CCPAP tumors did not show an enrichment of C:G > A:T mutations.
source: Interestingly, CCPAP tumors did not show an enrichment of C:G > A:T mutations, suggesting that the mutations arising in CCPAP are not the consequence of excess oxidative damage.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of the trinucleotide context of somatic mutations.

claim: Both CCPAP and ccRCC stained positively for PAS and were sensitive to diastase treatment (PAS-diastase), indicating the presence of cytoplasmic glycogen in both tumor types.
source: Both CCPAP and ccRCC stained positively for PAS and were sensitive to diastase treatment (PAS-diastase) (Figure 5E), indicating the presence of cytoplasmic glycogen in both tumor types.
evidence: The claim is supported by histochemical staining with PAS and PAS-diastase.

claim: Unlike ccRCC tumors which stained diffusely positive for Oil Red O, CCPAP tumors are Oil Red O negative.
source: However, unlike ccRCC tumors which stained diffusely positive for Oil Red O, CCPAP tumors are Oil Red O negative (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Oil Red O staining of tumor specimens.

claim: CCPAP and ccRCC tumors showed elevated levels of maltose, maltotriose, and maltotetraose (surrogates of glycogen content) compared to normal tissue.
source: Consistently, the RC13 metabolomics data indicated that CCPAP and ccRCC tumors showed elevated levels of maltose, maltotriose, and maltotetraose (surrogates of glycogen content) compared to normal tissue (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements of glycogen-related metabolites.

claim: CCPAP tumors are depleted of a variety of lipid classes compared to both ccRCC and adjacent normal kidney tissue.
source: Meanwhile, the RC13 metabolomics data showed that CCPAP tumors are depleted of a variety of lipid classes compared to both ccRCC and adjacent normal kidney tissue (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements of lipid classes.

claim: The cytoplasmic clarity in CCPAP tumors is due to reasons distinct from those in ccRCC tumors.
source: Together, these results indicate that CCPAP tumors do not contain high levels of intracytoplasmic lipids, and that the cytoplasmic clarity in CCPAP tumors is due to reasons distinct from those in ccRCC tumors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combination of Oil Red O staining and metabolomic data showing lipid depletion in CCPAP.

claim: CCPAP was initially described in kidneys with end stage renal disease (ESRD) (Tickoo et al., 2006).
source: CCPAP was initially described in kidneys with end stage renal disease (ESRD) (Tickoo et al., 2006), but was subsequently also described in patients with normal renal function (Rohan et al., 2011; Gobbo et al., 2008; Williamson et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature.

claim: CCPAP was subsequently described in patients with normal renal function (Rohan et al., 2011; Gobbo et al., 2008; Williamson et al., 2013).
source: CCPAP was initially described in kidneys with end stage renal disease (ESRD) (Tickoo et al., 2006), but was subsequently also described in patients with normal renal function (Rohan et al., 2011; Gobbo et al., 2008; Williamson et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature.

claim: CCPAP tumors are of low grade and stage, and are thought to be generally more indolent in nature (Gobbo et al., 2008; Ross et al., 2012).
source: Clinically, CCPAP tumors are of low grade and stage, and are thought to be generally more indolent in nature (Gobbo et al., 2008; Ross et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature describing clinical characteristics of CCPAP.

claim: CCPAP tumor cells have nuclei oriented away from the basement membrane in a linear fashion.
source: Morphologically, CCPAP tumor cells are unique in that their nuclei are oriented away from the basement membrane in a linear fashion, and they lack high-grade features including prominent nucleoli, mitotic figures, necrosis and sarcomatoid differentiation (Gobbo et al., 2008; Williamson et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature describing morphological features of CCPAP.

claim: CCPAP tumors lack high-grade features including prominent nucleoli, mitotic figures, necrosis and sarcomatoid differentiation (Gobbo et al., 2008; Williamson et al., 2013).
source: Morphologically, CCPAP tumor cells are unique in that their nuclei are oriented away from the basement membrane in a linear fashion, and they lack high-grade features including prominent nucleoli, mitotic figures, necrosis and sarcomatoid differentiation (Gobbo et al., 2008; Williamson et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature describing morphological features of CCPAP.

claim: CCPAP tumors show neither deletion of chromosome 3p nor mutation of VHL.
source: A handful of molecular studies have reported that cytogenetically, CCPAP tumors show neither deletion of chromosome 3p nor mutation of VHL, the characteristic molecular features of ccRCC.
evidence: The claim is based on prior molecular studies of CCPAP.

claim: CCPAP tumors do not exhibit gains of chromosomes 7 and 17, or loss of chromosome Y, as commonly described in papillary renal cell carcinoma (pRCC) (Rohan et al., 2011; Gobbo et al., 2008; Williamson et al., 2013).
source: They also do not exhibit gains of chromosomes 7 and 17, or loss of chromosome Y, as commonly described in papillary renal cell carcinoma (pRCC) (Rohan et al., 2011; Gobbo et al., 2008; Williamson et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature describing cytogenetic features of CCPAP.

claim: No genetic drivers of CCPAP have been reported (Rohan et al., 2011; Ross et al., 2012; Adam et al., 2011; Lawrie et al., 2014).
source: While several studies have now molecularly profiled CCPAP tumors, no genetic drivers of the disease have been reported (Rohan et al., 2011; Ross et al., 2012; Adam et al., 2011; Lawrie et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature that has profiled CCPAP without identifying genetic drivers.

claim: Nearly 8% of tumors in the institution's prospective sequencing cohort show no alterations in the 341 cancer-associated genes assayed by the clinical sequencing panel (Zehir et al., 2017).
source: Within our own institution's prospective sequencing cohort (Zehir et al., 2017), nearly 8% of tumors show no alterations in the 341 cancer-associated genes assayed by the clinical sequencing panel.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the institution's clinical sequencing cohort.

claim: Loss of fumarate hydratase (FH), succinate dehydrogenase (SDH), or isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) induces pathological accumulation of metabolites which potently inhibit alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent enzymes, inducing hypermethylation of the genome and a fundamental reprogramming of cellular identity (Wallace, 2012).
source: For example, loss of fumarate hydratase (FH), succinate dehydrogenase (SDH), or isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) induces pathological accumulation of metabolites which potently inhibit alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent enzymes, inducing hypermethylation of the genome and a fundamental reprogramming of cellular identity (Wallace, 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature on metabolic enzyme mutations.

claim: Otto Warburg observed that tumors take up and ferment large quantities of glucose to lactate in normoxia (i.e. aerobic glycolysis), leading him to propose that mitochondrial respiration defects are the underlying basis for cancer (Warburg, 1956a; Warburg, 1956b).
source: Similarly, Otto Warburg observed that tumors take up and ferment large quantities of glucose to lactate in normoxia (i.e. aerobic glycolysis), leading him to propose that mitochondrial respiration defects are the underlying basis for cancer (Warburg, 1956a; Warburg, 1956b).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of Warburg's historical observations.

claim: Not all tumors exhibit signatures of aerobic glycolysis.
source: Data from tumor genomics, imaging and metabolomics have now demonstrated that not all tumors exhibit signatures of aerobic glycolysis, and that alterations both intrinsic to mitochondria (e.g. mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) depletion) and extrinsic to mitochondria (e.g. increased glucose uptake) can induce aerobic glycolysis (Vyas et al., 2016; Zong et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of recent literature on tumor metabolism.

claim: A recent study described signals of positive selection for loss-of-function somatic mutations in mtDNA in thyroid cancers and chromophobe renal cell carcinomas (chRCC) (Grandhi et al., 2017).
source: A recent study described signals of positive selection for loss-of-function somatic mutations in mtDNA in thyroid cancers and chromophobe renal cell carcinomas (chRCC) (Grandhi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature on mtDNA mutations in cancer.

claim: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is characterized by biallelic loss of the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) tumor suppressor and subsequent activation of hypoxia inducible factor (HIF), suppressing mitochondrial respiration in favor of glycolytic metabolism.
source: For example, the most common RCC histology, clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), is characterized by biallelic loss of the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) tumor suppressor and subsequent activation of hypoxia inducible factor (HIF), suppressing mitochondrial respiration in favor of glycolytic metabolism.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ccRCC molecular characteristics.

claim: Chromophobe RCCs and renal oncocytomas are characterized by loss-of-function mutations in the mitochondrial genome resulting in accumulation of respiration-defective mitochondria (Joshi et al., 2015).
source: Similarly, chRCCs and renal oncocytomas are characterized by loss-of-function mutations in the mitochondrial genome resulting in accumulation of respiration-defective mitochondria (Joshi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature on chRCC and oncocytoma molecular characteristics.

claim: Inactivating mutations to genes essential for mtDNA replication, maintenance, and biosynthesis (e.g. POLG, TK2) can result in severe depletion of mtDNA and cause autosomally recessive heritable disorders (El-Hattab and Scaglia, 2013).
source: It is known that inactivating mutations to genes which are essential for mtDNA replication, maintenance, and biosynthesis (e.g. POLG, TK2) can result in severe depletion of mtDNA and cause autosomally recessive heritable disorders (El-Hattab and Scaglia, 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature on mtDNA depletion disorders.

claim: Sorbitol accumulation has been observed in the blood of patients with progressive external ophthalmoplegia (Esterhuizen et al., 2017).
source: Furthermore, studies of metabolomic changes associated with mitochondrial disease indicate that sorbitol accumulation is not a generic consequence of mitochondrial dysfunction, although its elevation has been observed in the blood of patients with progressive external ophthalmoplegia (Esterhuizen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature on metabolomic changes in mitochondrial disease.

claim: Lactate levels in CCPAP tumors were not elevated relative to normal tissue or ccRCC.
source: Specifically, lactate levels in CCPAP tumors were not elevated relative to normal tissue or ccRCC, nor were any other intermediates of glycolysis (Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements of lactate and glycolytic intermediates.

claim: ccRCC and papillary RCC (pRCC) are believed to derive from proximal tubule cells based on gene expression data.
source: On the basis of gene expression data, ccRCC and papillary RCC (pRCC) are believed to derive from proximal tubule cells, while chromophobe RCC (chRCC) is believed to arise from the distal tubule.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from gene expression data about cell-of-origin.

claim: Chromophobe RCC (chRCC) is believed to arise from the distal tubule based on gene expression data.
source: On the basis of gene expression data, ccRCC and papillary RCC (pRCC) are believed to derive from proximal tubule cells, while chromophobe RCC (chRCC) is believed to arise from the distal tubule.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from gene expression data about cell-of-origin.

claim: CCPAP tumors resemble cells of the collecting duct based on comparison of transcriptomic profiles with microdissected regions of mouse kidney (Cheval et al., 2012).
source: Doing so, we found that while ccRCC and pRCC tumors most resemble cells of the proximal tubule and chRCC tumors resemble cells of the distal tubule, CCPAP tumors resemble cells of the collecting duct (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of transcriptomic profiles with mouse kidney data.

claim: CCPAP tumors stain positive for the collecting duct marker 34BE12 (Cheval et al., 2012).
source: This is consistent with prior immunohistochemical findings showing that CCPAP tumors stain positive for the collecting duct marker 34BE12 (Cheval et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior immunohistochemical findings.

claim: CCPAP tumors display upregulated HIF1 protein as well as elevated levels of downstream HIF targets (CA9, GLUT1) by IHC staining despite wild-type VHL and TCEB1 (Rohan et al., 2011).
source: An interesting aspect of CCPAP RCC is that despite wild-type VHL and TCEB1, CCPAP tumors display upregulated HIF1 protein as well as elevated levels of downstream HIF targets (CA9, GLUT1) by IHC staining (Rohan et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior immunohistochemical findings.

claim: High levels of oxidative stress could inhibit prolyl hydroxylase (PHD) activity to prevent the hydroxylation of HIF and subsequent VHL-dependent degradation (Mansfield et al., 2005; Pan et al., 2007).
source: Conceivably, high levels of oxidative stress could inhibit prolyl hydroxylase (PHD) activity to prevent the hydroxylation of HIF and subsequent VHL-dependent degradation (Mansfield et al., 2005; Pan et al., 2007), which would be responsible for HIF activation in CCPAP.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on citation of prior literature on PHD inhibition by oxidative stress.

claim: Both HIF activation and oxidative stress have been shown to cause mtDNA depletion (Zhang et al., 2007; Mansouri et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2001; Suliman et al., 2003; Shokolenko et al., 2009).
source: Interestingly, both HIF activation and oxidative stress have been shown to cause mtDNA depletion (Zhang et al., 2007; Mansouri et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2001; Suliman et al., 2003; Shokolenko et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature on causes of mtDNA depletion.

claim: CCPAP tumors exhibit severe depletion of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and RNA.
source: In spite of a largely wild-type nuclear genome, CCPAP tumors exhibit severe depletion of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and RNA and high levels of oxidative stress, reflecting a shift away from respiratory metabolism.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including mtDNA copy number analysis and mtRNA expression analysis.

claim: CCPAP tumors exhibit high levels of oxidative stress.
source: In spite of a largely wild-type nuclear genome, CCPAP tumors exhibit severe depletion of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and RNA and high levels of oxidative stress, reflecting a shift away from respiratory metabolism.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements (elevated glutathione, ophthalmate) and immunohistochemical staining (8-oxo-dG).

claim: CCPAP tumors exhibit a distinct metabolic phenotype uniquely characterized by accumulation of the sugar alcohol sorbitol.
source: Moreover, CCPAP tumors exhibit a distinct metabolic phenotype uniquely characterized by accumulation of the sugar alcohol sorbitol.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements showing high sorbitol levels in CCPAP.

claim: CCPAP tumors reflect a shift away from respiratory metabolism.
source: In spite of a largely wild-type nuclear genome, CCPAP tumors exhibit severe depletion of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and RNA and high levels of oxidative stress, reflecting a shift away from respiratory metabolism.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combination of mtDNA/mtRNA depletion, downregulation of oxidative phosphorylation genes, and reduced levels of mitochondrial metabolites.

claim: Elevation of glutathione is generically observed across many RCC histologies, including but not limited to clear-cell, chromophobe, and oncocytomas (Hakimi et al., 2016; Gopal et al., 2018; Priolo et al., 2018).
source: Importantly, data from our group and others have repeatedly demonstrated that elevation of glutathione is generically observed across many RCC histologies, including but not limited to clear-cell, chromophobe, and oncocytomas (Hakimi et al., 2016; Gopal et al., 2018; Priolo et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature on glutathione levels in RCC.

claim: An elevated response to oxidative stress is particularly pronounced in CCPAP tumors.
source: Our data here suggests that an elevated response to oxidative stress is particularly pronounced in CCPAP tumors, but cannot be used to distinguish them from other histologies.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic and immunohistochemical data showing high levels of oxidative stress markers in CCPAP.
